What makes the polar regions so amazing?

Covered in ice, the polar regions are the coldest places on Earth. From polar bears and penguins to the auroras in the night sky, they're full of wonder.

content.alt: The wonders of the polar regions - Nature and science facts about the polar regions
content.text:
Nature and science facts about the polar regions

The Arctic is a frozen ocean, while the Antarctic is a continent covered in ice (and Antarctica is even colder). A polar bear's fur is made of hollow, transparent tubes that carry sunlight all the way to its skin to keep it warm, and emperor penguins survive the cold by huddling tightly together. The aurora is a glow that appears when particles from the Sun collide with the oxygen and nitrogen in the polar atmosphere, and it can shine in many colors like green, red, and purple.

Great points to explore together

Point out things like the Arctic vs. the Antarctic (ocean vs. continent), the polar bear (transparent fur), penguins (huddling), and the aurora (colors of light). Talking together about "Why do animals live even in such a cold place?" is a wonderful way to explore.

Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Touch some ice and imagine the cold of the polar regions, and try huddling together like penguins. Looking at photos and videos of auroras while talking about the colors of light makes it even more exciting.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What's the difference between the Arctic and the Antarctic?
A. The Arctic is a frozen ocean, and the Antarctic is a continent covered in ice. Antarctica is colder.

Q. Why do auroras happen?
A. Because particles from the Sun collide with the oxygen and nitrogen in the polar atmosphere and give off light. They come in many colors.

Q. How can we explore this at home?
A. Touch some ice, mimic a penguin huddle, and look at aurora photos while talking about the colors.
